title: Not a better wrestler
hook: someone may out-wrestle you, but not be kinder or more modest (Meditations 7.52)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was vine, which bears grapes and asks for nothing. Your line was content with right.

There's always someone better. Better at your job, better at tennis, better at small talk; better-looking, better paid. Your cousin got the promotion. Your old classmate wrote the book. The comparison machine never runs out of fuel, because there's always another name to feed it. Marcus Aurelius didn't try to smash the machine. In book seven he used a picture from the wrestling ground to switch it to a different contest entirely.
screen: `THERE'S ALWAYS SOMEONE BETTER.` → `THE COMPARISON MACHINE.` → `A DIFFERENT CONTEST.`

segments.voice: In Meditations seven, fifty-two, Marcus admits it plainly: someone else may be better at throwing an opponent. Some people really are more talented than you at things. But, he says, that person is not more devoted to the common good. Not more modest. Not better trained to meet whatever happens. Not more considerate of other people's faults. Four contests, and none of them depends on your body, your luck or your talent. Marcus doesn't kill the urge to compete; he moves it. If you're going to outdo people, outdo them in the things entirely in your power. You can't choose to be taller or quicker. You can choose to be more patient with a coworker's mistakes. In that contest anyone can win, and nobody has to lose. There's a trick hiding inside it: when you compete in kindness, the other person benefits from your winning. Paul's letter to the Romans has a neighboring line, in the King James words: "in honour preferring one another." Different tradition, with its own reasons and its own meaning. So when the comparison machine starts up, let it. Then ask it a different question. Not who's better. Who's kinder, today?
screen: `SOMEONE WRESTLES BETTER.` · `NOT MORE MODEST OR CONSIDERATE.` · `COMPETE IN WHAT'S YOURS.` · `A CONTEST WHERE OTHERS WIN TOO.` · then, large: `OUT-KIND THEM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you tend to compare yourself to, and let the comparison come, with its sting. Then change the contest: could I be more patient than them today, more modest, more forgiving of others' mistakes? Pick one, and picture it in one real moment.
Mat. Someone else may beat you there, Marcus admits, but no one can stop you being kinder or more modest. Today's word.
Your line: out-kind them. In that contest, nobody has to lose. That's day five hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes redirect envy into a contest of character, asking who can be most patient or considerate in a situation rather than who is most talented.

notes: Editor review (y2 pass): Romans 12:10 had been given in modern-translation wording ('outdo one another in showing honor'); now quoted from the KJV and cited, without claiming Paul and Marcus share one insight. Cut the claim that Marcus felt envy, the unsourced note on wrestling in his world, the 'favorite words' superlative, and 'most patient person in the room' (also day 594's review).

Meditations 7.52 paraphrased: another may be more expert in throwing his opponent, but not more social, nor more modest, nor better disciplined to meet all that happens, nor more considerate of the faults of neighbors. Confirm.
